title: Where Life Begins: A Sub‑Elementary Framework for Agency in Organized Matter
content:
Abstract

Life has no universally accepted definition across scientific disciplines. Biological, chemical, and philosophical frameworks each impose criteria that reflect their own assumptions and observational limits. This paper develops an alternative approach grounded in a sub‑elementary substrate—described in prior work as composed of Zot particles—that underlies all known matter. Within this framework, life is not a discrete threshold but a continuum emerging from the organization and dynamics of this substrate across scales. Atoms, as coherent configurations of these sub‑elementary units, exhibit minimal but non‑zero agency and therefore constitute the simplest living systems. Increasing structural complexity—from atoms to molecules, proteins, cells, and organisms—corresponds to increasing degrees of agency. This perspective reframes life as a universal property of organized matter rather than a phenomenon restricted to biological systems.

1. Introduction

Attempts to define life have historically been discipline‑specific. Biology emphasizes metabolism, reproduction, and homeostasis; chemistry focuses on self‑organization and reaction networks; philosophy invokes intentionality or emergent properties. These definitions reflect the conceptual boundaries of their respective fields rather than a unified underlying principle.

A different foundation emerges when matter is understood as arising from a deeper substrate composed of sub‑elementary constituents. In the Zot framework, these constituents—Zots—form the basis from which subatomic particles, atoms, and larger structures arise. If the substrate itself exhibits structured behavior, then life may not originate at the cellular or molecular level but at the atomic level, where the first coherent assemblies appear.

This paper develops a framework in which life is treated as a continuum of organization rooted in the dynamics of this underlying structure. Agency—defined as the capacity of a system to maintain coherence, respond to conditions, and participate in organized interactions—is examined as the fundamental property that scales upward into biological life.

2. Life as a Continuum of Sub‑Elementary Organization

2.1. Minimal Life at the Atomic Scale

Atoms are not indivisible units but stable configurations of deeper constituents. Their persistence, internal motion, and responsiveness to environmental conditions constitute a minimal form of agency. This agency is not biological, nor does it imply subjective experience. Rather, it reflects the capacity of atomic structures to:

  • maintain coherent organization,
  • respond to external influences,
  • undergo transformation while preserving identity,
  • and participate in structured interactions.

Subatomic components—protons, neutrons, and electrons—function analogously to internal parts of a biological cell. They contribute to the atom’s behavior but do not independently constitute living systems. The atom, as the smallest coherent assembly of Zots, represents the first level at which life can be meaningfully defined.

2.2. Increasing Complexity Across Scales

Life increases in complexity as sub‑elementary units assemble into larger structures. The progression is continuous:


Zots→Subatomic Structures→Atoms→Molecules→Proteins→Cells→Organisms.



Each level introduces new emergent properties, but none represent a discontinuous transition from non‑life to life. Instead, life becomes more elaborate as structural and functional organization increases.

This view contrasts with traditional biological definitions, which treat life as a binary state. Here, life is a gradient that begins at the atomic level and extends upward through all forms of organized matter.

3. Agency as a Scale‑Dependent Property

3.1. Substrate‑Level Agency

Agency refers to the capacity of a system to sustain structure, respond to perturbations, and participate in organized interactions. At the atomic level, this capacity is minimal and expressed through internal dynamics. Atoms maintain coherence, reorganize under pressure, and form bonds that reflect structured patterns of interaction.

3.2. Emergent Agency Across Scales

As structures become more complex, their agency becomes more elaborate. Molecules exhibit selective reactivity; proteins fold and function according to internal constraints; cells regulate internal states and interact with their environment; organisms coordinate large‑scale behaviors.

Agency is therefore not a single property but a family of related capacities that scale with complexity. It is not subjective, introspective, or tied to any particular biological architecture. Instead, it is a structural and dynamical property of organized matter.

4. Structural Analogies Across Scales

4.1. Social Organization as a Macro‑Scale Parallel

The hierarchical organization observed in physical systems has a natural analogy in human social structures. Individuals form households; households form communities; communities form cities; cities form nations. Each level introduces new forms of coordination, regulation, and collective behavior that cannot be reduced to the properties of the individuals alone.

This mirrors the progression:



Zots→Subatomic Structures→Atoms→Molecules→Proteins→Cells→Organisms.



Just as a city exhibits properties—traffic flow, governance, culture—that do not exist at the level of individual citizens, a cell exhibits properties that do not exist at the level of individual molecules. Both are examples of emergent agency arising from hierarchical organization.

4.2. Fish in Water, Atoms in a Substrate

A second analogy helps visualize the substrate itself. Fish live within water, shaped by currents they do not perceive directly. Atoms, in this framework, exist within a pervasive medium of sub‑elementary constituents. The comparison is not literal—atoms do not swim, and the substrate is not a fluid in the classical sense—but the analogy illustrates a structural parallel: both systems consist of entities embedded in a medium whose dynamics influence their behavior.

Just as the properties of water shape the possibilities for aquatic life, the properties of the underlying substrate shape the possibilities for atomic and molecular organization. This analogy provides an intuitive picture of how life can exist across scales without requiring a sharp boundary between living and non‑living matter.

4.3. Emergence Without Discontinuity

In both physical and social systems, each level depends on the organization of the level below it. No single transition marks the “beginning” of life or agency; instead, each level adds new constraints, capabilities, and modes of interaction.

These analogies illustrate that life, like social organization, is best understood as a continuum rather than a binary state.

5. A Universe Immersed in Structure

5.1. Matter Embedded in a Sub‑Elementary Medium

In this framework, the universe is not an empty vacuum but a medium filled with sub‑elementary constituents. Atoms are suspended within this substrate, and their interactions reflect the dynamics of the surrounding medium. From a sufficiently distant perspective, matter appears as a sparse distribution of organized structures within a pervasive field.

5.2. Interconnectedness Across Scales

Zooming inward, the apparent emptiness between atoms dissolves into a dense network of interactions. The substrate forms the connective tissue of the universe, linking all structures through continuous motion and reorganization. Life, in this context, is not an isolated phenomenon but a natural expression of the universe’s capacity to organize itself.

6. Implications for the Study of Life

6.1. Redefining Life

This framework suggests that life is not restricted to biological systems. Instead, it is a universal property of organized matter. Biological life represents a high‑complexity expression of principles already present at the atomic level.

6.2. Agency as the Unifying Concept

Agency provides a more precise and scalable concept than traditional biological criteria. It avoids subjective interpretation and applies uniformly across scales. It captures the essential continuity between atomic organization and biological function.

6.3. Toward a Unified Framework

By grounding life and agency in the same sub‑elementary substrate, this approach offers a unified perspective that bridges physics and biology. It reframes life as a structural and dynamical property of matter rather than a phenomenon that emerges only at high complexity.

7. Conclusion

Life begins at the atomic level because atoms are structured, self‑sustaining configurations of deeper constituents. Their minimal agency constitutes the simplest form of life. As structures assemble into increasingly complex forms, life becomes more elaborate but never fundamentally changes in nature. This framework positions life not as an exceptional phenomenon but as a natural consequence of the universe’s capacity for self‑organization.
